course.title: Cognition and Computation
course.description: This seminar introduces students to the philosophical foundations of cognitive science. Our focus will be the core hypothesis that cognition is rooted in computations carried out in the brain. We will approach these issues through the lens of classic theoretical texts from the last 75 years, including works by Craik, Turing, Chomsky, Marr, Fodor, and others. This literature will be interleaved with contemporary real-world cases from cognitive science (face recognition, spatial maps in the hippocampus, and semantic priming) and from computer science (finite-state machines, neural networks, and transformer architectures). The last three weeks of the course will focus on understanding contemporary AI models, and comparing them to human cognition.

announcements.title: Cross-enrolling with Phil 133.
announcements.html: I will be concurrently teaching Philosophy 133 (Computational Theory of Mind), which covers much of the formal background in the theory of computation. Graduate students are more than welcome to attend and enroll (or audit). The two courses will be highly complementary. Course website: makingminds.org

items.title: Short paper
fields: pick one article we’ve read, and isolate one key idea or argument from that article to discuss.
(1) Present and explain the idea or argument; (2) identify some weakness or challenge for that view; (3) briefly, indicate some way out of the problem.
the challenge in (2) could be a counterexample, a lacuna, a missed opportunity, etc.
title, date, name, bibliography, and page numbering.
as a PDF, by email to gabriel.greenberg@gmail.com, with your name in the file name (e.g., Lastname – Short paper.pdf).

items.title: Long paper outline
fields: a working title; your thesis, in a sentence or two; a section-by-section plan; and the main readings you will engage with.
title, date, name, bibliography, and page numbering.
as a PDF, by email to gabriel.greenberg@gmail.com, with your name in the file name (e.g., Lastname – Outline.pdf).

items.title: Long paper meeting
fields: Once you’ve sent your outline, schedule a meeting with me (office hours or Zoom) to talk it through. Earlier is better.

items.title: Long paper
fields: pick a topic of your choice from the reading, or from areas that are (more or less) related to the course.
your choice. Be sure to have a clear thesis, consider possible objections to your claim, and include multiple detailed examples to illustrate. Prioritize depth over breadth.
include at least two diagrams or figures, with captions, inserted inline (not as an appendix). The long paper may build upon the short paper.
title, date, name, bibliography, and page numbering.
as a PDF, by email to gabriel.greenberg@gmail.com, with your name in the file name (e.g., Lastname – Long paper.pdf).

policies.label: Reading
policies.html: Do the main reading before each session. Recommended and optional readings are for going deeper, and are a good place to start looking for paper topics.

policies.label: Attendance and participation
policies.html: Come every week having done the reading, ready to discuss. If you have to miss a session, let me know in advance.

policies.label: Extensions
policies.html: Ask by email before the deadline; short extensions are normally fine. Final grades are due 12/21, so long papers can’t come in after Tue 12/15 unless we’ve arranged an Incomplete.

policies.label: AI tools
policies.html: Fine as a tutor: to explain background (e.g., how a transformer works), to work through examples, or to find literature (check every reference yourself). Not fine for writing: drafting or rewriting your prose, or generating the arguments and objections in your papers. Language models are also a subject of this course, so if you probe a model as part of a paper, that’s welcome — just say what you did.

policies.label: Auditors
policies.html: Auditors are welcome. Please do the reading and come regularly; no written work is required.

policies.label: Accommodations
policies.html: If you need academic accommodations, contact the Center for Accessible Education as early in the quarter as you can, and let me know.

policies.label: Academic integrity
policies.html: Your papers must be your own work, with every source cited. UCLA’s Student Conduct Code applies.
